subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
Monday
Fourth planning meeting and Baljeet hasn't said a word. Again. She takes pages of notes, and her test reports are the cleanest on the floor, but in the meeting she just looks at her laptop.
I remember that. My first year here, I thought everyone could hear how little I knew.
Tuesday
During the release discussion I said, 'Baljeet, you tested the payment flow. What did you see?' She went red, then said the retry screen froze on slow networks. Two people hadn't known. It changed the plan.
Afterwards, at the coffee machine, I told her I barely spoke for my first three months. She looked surprised. 'You?'
Thursday
In the team update I said, 'The retry bug, Baljeet caught that. It would have hit thousands of users.'
Today she raised her hand, by herself, to ask about the deadline. Small thing. Not small.
Lokesh

qa.q: What did Baljeet say about the payment flow?
qa.a: She said the retry screen froze on slow networks.

qa.q: How can you tell Baljeet felt nervous when Lokesh first asked her view?
qa.a: She went red before answering, which suggests she was uneasy about speaking in the meeting.

qa.q: Which three things did Lokesh do that helped Baljeet speak up?
qa.a: Lokesh invited her view on something she knew, shared that everyone once felt lost, and gave her specific credit in the team update.

qa.q: How might Baljeet see Lokesh after learning Lokesh barely spoke at first too?
qa.a: She may see Lokesh as someone who understands, which makes it feel safer for her to speak.

grounding: It shows a senior colleague noticing a capable, silent newcomer and helping her find a voice by inviting her view, sharing past doubts and giving specific credit.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
Chaitanya: hey Lalit, got a sec?
Lalit: yes sorry, did I mess something up?
Chaitanya: no! the opposite
Chaitanya: I read your churn analysis in the shared doc last night. the bit about customers leaving after the second price change. nobody had split it that way before
Lalit: oh. I wasn't sure it was right
Chaitanya: it's right. I checked
Chaitanya: why didn't you bring it up in the review today?
Lalit: everyone seemed to know what they were talking about. I didn't want to waste time
Chaitanya: honestly, my first two months here I didn't say a single thing in meetings. I thought they'd find out I was a fluke 🙂
Lalit: really?
Chaitanya: really. would you walk us through the churn split on Thursday? 5 minutes. I'll introduce it
Lalit: ok. I'll try
Chaitanya: you'll be fine. it's good work

qa.q: What part of the churn analysis did Chaitanya say nobody had split that way before?
qa.a: The bit about customers leaving after the second price change.

qa.q: Why didn't Lalit bring the analysis up in the review?
qa.a: Lalit felt everyone else seemed to know more and worried that speaking up would waste time.

qa.q: What makes Chaitanya's approach likely to help Lalit find a voice?
qa.a: Chaitanya gives specific credit, shares their own early silence, and offers a short, supported slot to present.

qa.q: What would change if Chaitanya had only said 'speak up more' in the meeting?
qa.a: Lalit might feel exposed or scolded and stay even quieter, without the reassurance and specific praise that made speaking feel safe.

grounding: It shows a senior colleague inviting a capable, silent newcomer to share work, admitting their own early silence and giving specific credit.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
At the farm science centre outside Latur, Omkar had run the Monday meeting for eleven years, and noticed that Zainab, the new soil scientist, never spoke. Yet her field reports were sharp; she was the one who had spotted the salt build-up in the Jadhav family's plot.
This Monday, when the talk turned to the drip trial, Omkar said, "Zainab, you've walked those fields more than any of us this month. What did you see?"
She hesitated, then spoke for two minutes about waterlogging at the lower end. The room went quiet, then the senior officer nodded.
After the meeting Omkar walked with her to the jeep. "My first year here, I didn't say a word in these meetings for six months. I thought everyone knew more. Your salt report was the best catch of the season. Say that sort of thing out loud."
Zainab laughed, a little embarrassed. "Okay. Next Monday."

qa.q: What had Zainab spotted in the Jadhav family's plot?
qa.a: The salt build-up.

qa.q: What did Omkar feel on noticing that Zainab never spoke?
qa.a: Omkar felt concerned, with a touch of recognition, since a capable newcomer was hiding sharp work the way Omkar once did.

qa.q: Which of Omkar's moves helped Zainab find her voice?
qa.a: Inviting her view with a specific question, sharing an early silent year, and naming the salt report as the season's best catch.

qa.q: What is it like for Zainab to speak in the meeting?
qa.a: Nervous at first, then encouraging, as the room listens and the senior officer nods.

grounding: A senior colleague notices a capable newcomer who never speaks, invites her view, shares an early struggle and gives specific credit.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
Wanjiru had been at the transit planning office in Toronto for nine years, long enough to recognise the look on Tuan's face in the Thursday meetings: pen moving, mouth shut. He had been there three months. His route analysis for the east-end buses was the cleanest work she'd seen from a new hire, and nobody in the room knew it was his.
So on Thursday, when the group got stuck on transfer times, she said, "Tuan ran these numbers last week. Tuan, what did you find?"
He cleared his throat and explained, quietly at first, then faster.
Afterwards she caught him at the coffee machine. "In my first year I wrote whole reports and let my manager present them. I thought everyone here was smarter. They weren't. Your transfer map is clearer than anything we've had in years."
Tuan looked at the floor, then grinned. "Could I present the map next month?"

qa.q: How long had Wanjiru been at the transit planning office?
qa.a: Nine years.

qa.q: What was Wanjiru thinking when she recognised the look on Tuan's face?
qa.a: She felt concerned and protective, remembering her own silence and worried that his good work was invisible.

qa.q: What did Wanjiru do that helped Tuan speak?
qa.a: She invited him by name in the meeting, told him about her own first year, and praised the transfer map specifically.

qa.q: How might Tuan feel when he asks to present the map?
qa.a: He feels encouraged and bolder, trusting now that his work is valued.

grounding: A senior planner notices a capable newcomer's silence, invites his view, shares her own early doubt and gives specific credit.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
In the staffroom of the Gangtok school, the Friday meeting always ran the same way: the loud teachers talked, the tea went cold, the new ones listened. Yogesh, who had taught physics there for fifteen years, noticed that Pema, the new geography teacher, never said a word. Yet her Class 7 had just made the best map project the school had displayed in years.
At this meeting, when the principal asked for ideas for environment week, Yogesh said, "Pema's class mapped every water source around the school. Pema, could that be a starting point?"
Pema flushed, then explained the idea in a few quick sentences. Two teachers asked for her worksheet.
Later, rinsing his cup, Yogesh said, "In my first year here I didn't speak in these meetings till March. Your map is the reason my students keep talking about the stream."
Pema smiled into her tea. "I thought nobody had noticed it."

qa.q: What did Pema's class map?
qa.a: Every water source around the school.

qa.q: What might Yogesh have felt noticing Pema's silence?
qa.a: He probably felt concerned and a bit of recognition, since he stayed quiet in his own first year.

qa.q: Which of Yogesh's actions helped Pema speak up?
qa.a: He named her project to the principal, asked her view directly, and later shared his own quiet first year and specific credit.

qa.q: What is it like for Pema to hear that her project was noticed?
qa.a: She feels surprised and relieved, having believed nobody noticed her work 😊

grounding: A senior teacher notices a capable new colleague who never speaks, invites her idea, shares his own early silence and gives specific credit.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
Hi Harsha,
A short note after today's review. I noticed you didn't say anything in the meeting again, and I also noticed that the fix everyone was praising, the retry logic in the billing service, came from your code on Monday. I made sure to tell the team lead that afterwards, with your name on it.
Can I tell you something? In my first year here, I didn't speak in a single review for four months. I was sure everyone knew more than me. A senior called Latha asked me directly, "Pradeep, what do you think?" and waited. That one question changed a lot.
So here's my version: in Thursday's meeting, I'm going to ask you to explain the retry logic for two minutes. You know it better than anyone. If that feels like too much, tell me, and we'll do it together.
Pradeep

qa.q: Whose code contained the retry logic everyone praised?
qa.a: Harsha's code from Monday.

qa.q: Why does Pradeep want to help Harsha speak up?
qa.a: Pradeep remembers feeling unsure and silent for four months, and cares that Harsha's good work is going unheard.

qa.q: Which parts of Pradeep's plan help Harsha find a voice?
qa.a: Giving specific credit to the team lead, sharing Pradeep's own silent first year, and inviting a two-minute explanation with an offer to do it together.

qa.q: What might Harsha feel reading this note?
qa.a: Harsha may feel seen and a bit nervous, but encouraged by the credit and the offer of support.

grounding: Shows a senior colleague noticing a capable, silent newcomer and helping by giving specific credit, sharing their own early doubts and inviting their view.
